rose-island.story:
The Republic of Rose Island was a platform in the Adriatic Sea, nearly 12 kilometres off Rimini, Italy, whose builder declared it an independent country. Italian territorial waters, the coastal belt a state fully controls, ended a few hundred metres short of it. Rimini is a beach resort, so summer tourists were close at hand.
Its builder was Giorgio Rosa, an engineer from Bologna who liked engineering experiments and disliked the bureaucracy around property. He had the idea in 1958 and spent about two years studying how to fix a structure to the seabed. His method, which he patented, was to build a frame on the beach, float it out, lower hollow pillars to the bottom, drive steel tubes through them into the sea floor and fill them with cement. The sea and weather allowed only a few working hours a week, so construction took years. The result was a 400-square-metre deck on nine pylons, with a well reaching fresh water 280 metres below the sea floor.
Late in 1966 the Rimini harbour office asked him to stop, partly because nearby areas had been leased to the state energy company ENI. Police also took an interest. He carried on and opened to the public in summer 1967, with a bar, restaurant, nightclub, shop and post office, and started a second storey. On 1 May 1968 he declared independence and made himself president. The state's official name was in Esperanto, the invented international language, and its government was made up of Rosa's relatives and acquaintances. Its currency, the mill, was set equal to the Italian lira, but no coins or notes are known, only stamps. It used an anthem from a Wagner opera. Nobody is known to have lived there apart from a guard and his partner.
He held a press conference in June. Italian officials suspected that the point was to take money from tourists without paying tax on it. Rosa met an official of the military intelligence service, with no result. On 26 June, about eight weeks after the declaration, police and tax officers came by boat, took control and blockaded the platform. Rosa telegraphed Italy's president, Giuseppe Saragat, and got no reply. Questions were asked in parliament, and he received several offers to buy the platform.
In August the merchant marine ministry ordered him to demolish it, and his appeal failed. Everything movable was taken ashore in November. The platform survived two explosive charges in February 1969, and a storm sank it on 26 February. Rosa issued stamps showing the destruction. He died in 2017, having approved a film about the episode, and Rose Island was released on Netflix in 2020.
The Council of State, Italy's top administrative court, held the claims of independence and sovereignty unfounded. Its reasoning turned on the person and not the place. Italian citizens remain subject to Italian law even outside Italy. Standing outside territorial waters therefore did not free an Italian who built, ran and profited from a platform there. So distance from the coast did not end the duties Rosa owed to the country of his citizenship. The platform was also near enough to Rimini for police boats to reach it as easily as tourists did.

minerva.story:
The Republic of Minerva was an attempt in 1972 to create a new country on the Minerva Reefs, two ring-shaped coral reefs in the South Pacific between Fiji and Tonga, about 270 miles from Tonga's capital. They were named after the whaling ship Minerva, wrecked there in 1829. The reef surface stands about three feet out of the water at low tide and about four feet under at high tide, so it was a hazard to ships and nobody lived on it.
Its backer was Michael Oliver, a Nevada real estate developer and coin dealer, and a concentration camp survivor. In 1968 he published A New Constitution for a New Country, a model for a state with very limited government paid for voluntarily. He wanted a country with no taxation, welfare, subsidies or economic intervention, where people could do as they pleased if they did not infringe on others' rights. Income would come from fees paid by banks and multinational companies that based themselves there.
He raised money from about 2,000 investors through a body called the Ocean Life Research Foundation, with offices in New York and London. He first tried to buy an island from a government, and no one would sell sovereignty, so the group chose to build its own land. Accounts of the construction differ. Some say barges or a dredging ship brought sand from Australia, while another describes a small party sailing from Fiji in January 1971 with coral wrapped in chicken wire, concrete blocks and rubble. The result was two tiny islands with a stone platform and a flag, a torch on a blue background. The plan was for a resort called Sea City with 30,000 people. No one actually lived there. Minerva dollar coins were struck, including a 35-dollar piece.
A declaration of independence went to neighbouring states and about a hundred nations on 19 January 1972. Morris "Bud" Davis was named provisional president and ran the republic from his living room in Gustine, California.
Neighbours reacted because of what it might mean for them. Tonga had not included the reefs in its 1887 territorial claim, and Fiji's prime minister asked what would stop such people claiming land in Fiji. Australia also objected to a private state in its region. At a conference on 24 February, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Nauru, Samoa and the Cook Islands backed a Tongan claim. Tonga proclaimed the reefs and the waters within 12 miles as its own on 15 June. An expedition arrived on 18 June. On 21 June the king, Taufaʻahau Tupou IV, sailed out on the royal yacht with soldiers, a convict work party and a four-piece brass band. He tore down the flag and read a proclamation of sovereignty, and the platform was dismantled within hours. In one account a fight between two of the convicts left one of them dead. In September the South Pacific Forum named Tonga as the only possible owner, without explicitly recognising its title.
Oliver then dismissed Davis and the project collapsed. He went on to back separatists on Abaco in the Bahamas and on Vanuatu, where Papua New Guinean soldiers put down the revolt in 1980. One account also names Australian troops.
The case shows the weakness of the empty-reef idea. International law makes land that no state holds open to the first state that takes it, and a private person is not a state. Once an unclaimed reef became a problem, a neighbour could simply claim it, and the region agreed. A sand pile with no population, army or recognition had nothing to set against that.

abaco.story:
The Abaco Islands are an inhabited chain in the northern Bahamas, the group of Atlantic islands just east of Florida. In the early 1970s the Bahamas was preparing to leave British rule, and it became independent in 1973. Some white residents of Abaco objected to living under black rule. The Abaco Independence Movement was founded in mid-1973 (sources differ between June and August) by Chuck Hall and Bert Williams, with the stated aim of self-determination for Abaco through legal and peaceful political action, within a federal Bahamas.
Hall and Williams contacted Michael Oliver, a real-estate millionaire based in the United States. Oliver's Phoenix Foundation backed libertarian attempts to create new states, meaning states with very little government. In 1972 it had piled sand on a reef in the South Pacific and declared the Republic of Minerva, and that June, about five months after the declaration, Tonga sent an expedition and raised its own flag there. Abaco was the foundation's next attempt, and in 1980 it backed a breakaway on Espiritu Santo in Vanuatu.
The foundation paid for a newsletter, The Abaco Independent. The movement proposed placing all Crown land on Abaco, meaning land held by the government, in a trust. Each citizen would receive a one-acre home lot and a share of revenue from land sales and leases, and the trust would help develop a 60-square-mile free trade zone, where goods move without customs duties.
The first convention, on 23 February 1974, was addressed by John Hospers, the 1972 presidential candidate of the American Libertarian Party, who was later refused entry to the Bahamas. Around May 1974 reports appeared of a group of "20th Century Revolutionaries" and the movement denounced it. In February 1975 Esquire magazine reported that a rising was being planned, and the American arms dealer and mercenary Mitchell WerBell said Abaco would declare independence on its own. It was claimed that WerBell was managing and financing the movement and recruiting mercenaries.
No arrests followed, but the connection, which included visits to WerBell's Georgia estate, damaged the group. In March 1975 it renamed itself the Abaco Home Rule Movement, denied any military aims and published a draft constitution for an Abaco Commonwealth. In the 1977 general election the governing Progressive Liberal Party won 30 of 38 seats, including one on Abaco itself. That effectively ended the movement, and its newspaper stopped that year.
Abaco remains part of the Bahamas. The case shows the limits of a breakaway on an island where people already live under an elected government. Foreign money could print a newsletter and a constitution, but the plan needed local votes, and its ties to an arms dealer cost it support.

hutt-river.story:
The Principality of Hutt River was a farm in Western Australia, 517 kilometres north of Perth near the town of Northampton, whose owner declared it an independent country. It lasted 50 years as a micronation. A micronation is a tiny self-declared country that no government recognises.
It began with wheat. Leonard Casley, a farmer, had about 4,000 hectares of crop ready to harvest when new state government quotas allowed him to sell only about 40 hectares' worth. Five families who farmed at Hutt River banded together, and Casley protested to the governor of Western Australia, without result. He says a bill was then introduced to take the families' land under compulsory purchase laws. On 21 April 1970 he declared his 75-square-kilometre farm the independent Hutt River Province, saying that international law allowed it, while also saying he stayed loyal to Queen Elizabeth II.
He built his case from legal fragments. A letter from the governor-general's office once addressed him as "Administrator of the Hutt River Province", and he treated that as recognition. He began calling himself Prince Leonard because he believed a 1495 English law protected a ruling king from treason charges. He also believed the federal government had two years to respond to his declaration, and he said its silence gave him self-rule in practice from 21 April 1972. Australian courts did not accept these arguments.
The farm became a regional tourist attraction, and Casley said he kept selling wheat in defiance of the quota. He issued a currency, more than 50 sets of stamps and passports, none of which any government accepted. Visitors got entry visas, and an anthem was written in 1984.
Australia still expected him to pay tax. In February 1977 he was convicted for failing to give tax documents to the Australian Taxation Office. That December he declared war on Australia and ended the war days later, apparently on the theory that a government must respect an undefeated nation under the Geneva Conventions. In 1978 he lost an appeal over running a shop without a permit. When others sued him over a land deal and a printing bill, he did not claim to be beyond the courts' reach. In 2007 the High Court of Australia rejected his attempt to appeal, calling his arguments fatuous, frivolous and vexatious, a phrase for a case with no legal merit. In June 2017 a judge of the Supreme Court of Western Australia rejected the argument that the court had no power over Hutt River and ordered Leonard to pay A$2.7 million and his son Arthur A$242,000 in unpaid tax.
Leonard handed over to his youngest son, Graeme, in 2017 and died in February 2019, leaving a tax debt of about A$2.5 million. In December 2019, citing lower farm income and fewer tourists, the principality said it would close to visitors from the end of January 2020. On 3 August 2020 Graeme dissolved it, citing hard times in the pandemic, and the farm went on sale.
For decades Australia left the farm alone, apart from the tax cases. Its courts treated the Casleys as Australian taxpayers throughout, and the debt passed to the founder's son.

set.pop: 26 at the end by The Guardian's count; another account gives 23

liberland.story:
Liberland is a self-declared country on a strip of flood-prone forest on the Danube river, between Croatia and Serbia. It is the best-known modern attempt to found a state on land said to be unclaimed, and it has become the standard test of whether that argument works.
The background is a border disagreement left by the break-up of Yugoslavia. Serbia places the border on the deepest channel of the river. Croatia uses old land records that follow the river's 19th-century course, which has since moved. That left pockets on the west bank that Serbia does not claim and that Croatia does not treat as settled Croatian land. On 13 April 2015 the Czech politician Vit Jedlicka, a member of the Czech Party of Free Citizens, planted a flag on the largest pocket, 7 square kilometres of floodplain called Gornja Siga, and declared a state where paying tax would be optional. He argued that no nation claimed the land, so he could take it as terra nullius, land belonging to no state. The land has no infrastructure or residents, and a journalist who visited in April 2015 found one abandoned house.
Croatia does not accept the argument. It treats the land as part of an unsettled border dispute and says the land should go to Croatia or Serbia after arbitration, a process in which a neutral panel settles a dispute, and not to a third party. It says visitors must obey Croatian law, it has been detaining them since May 2015, and it has frequently blocked access. That May, Jedlicka spent a night in custody and was fined. Serbia calls the project frivolous and says it is no threat so long as it stays on the western bank. So its people work from elsewhere. Jedlicka lives in Prague, supporters gather in Serbian villages and on houseboats, and the group has hired a lobbyist in the United States, registered with the Justice Department, to seek recognition.
The country has mostly existed online. Its planned currency is a cryptocurrency called Merit, with bitcoin and gold also promoted, and a registry and voting system would run on a blockchain, an online shared ledger. Passports are sold to paying supporters, at $10,000 by Wikipedia's account and at $5,000 or equivalent for full citizenship by Wired's. Wired magazine reported that 700,000 people had registered support and about 6,000 were paying e-residents, meaning members who hold an online form of citizenship, and that about 1,000 had paid by 2023. These counts come from the group, and RFE/RL, a US-funded news service, could not confirm the number of citizenship requests on its website.
In August 2023, after Croatia joined the Schengen area of free travel in Europe, supporters built wooden shelters. Police arrested Jedlicka on 9 September and banned him from Croatia for five years. On 21 September a private company, watched by police, took down and removed the camp, and the settlers moved to houseboats and a village on the Serbian side. Supporters came back in November 2023 and camped on a river island inside the claimed area. In March 2024 more than 200 people reached the land during a landing attempt by Jedlicka. On 5 October 2024 the group held its first congress election, run on a blockchain.
Nobody lives on the land, and no recognised state accepts it as a country. The legal point is that two states disagreeing about a border is not the same as no state having a claim. Even if the land had been truly unclaimed, the case law on empty land concerns states taking it, and a private declaration needs others to accept it. Croatia's position is the one that counts on the ground, because it controls the bank.

prospera-zede.story:
Próspera is a private business zone with its own rules on Roatán, a Caribbean island off the north coast of Honduras. It is the most fully developed recent attempt to get a country to hand over lawmaking to a private company, and its fate is being decided in court.
The legal path began in Honduras's own politics. An earlier plan, called Special Development Regions, was struck down as a breach of sovereignty, the country's right to govern itself. In 2013 Honduras changed its constitution to allow Zones for Employment and Economic Development (ZEDEs), areas with their own laws, courts and taxes.
Erick Brimen, a Venezuelan-born fund manager, applied in 2017 and built Próspera with American venture capital, through a Delaware company. The company appoints four of the nine members of the zone's council, and decisions need a two-thirds majority, which gives it a veto. The zone offers single-digit taxes, its own civil and commercial rules and a court of retired Arizona judges who hear cases online. Honduran criminal law still applies inside it. It is one of three ZEDEs in Honduras and had about 2,000 people in 2024. Neighbours in the village of Crawfish Rock feared losing their land, and the project became a national issue.
Politics then turned. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal of the ZEDE law in April 2022, saying Honduras was recovering its sovereignty. On 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court declared the ZEDE laws unconstitutional, with retroactive effect, which means that they count as invalid from the start. That reach back in time is argued both ways. Brimen points to Article 96 of the Honduran constitution, which says a law has no retroactive effect except in some criminal cases, and to treaty promises he says protect the investments for at least 50 years. The constitutional lawyer Juan Carlos Barrientos answers that Article 96 concerns penalties such as prison and fines, and that the constitutional chamber may apply its rulings to the past.
Its owners had already claimed about $10.8 billion from Honduras at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), a World Bank body that decides disputes between investors and governments. They relied on a legal stability agreement promising fixed rules and on CAFTA-DR, a trade treaty between the United States and Central American countries. Honduras left ICSID in August 2024. Under President Nasry Asfura, who took office in January 2026, it rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026, and that return covers the country only from that date onward. Honduran officials said in October 2025 that the claim had dropped to $1.63 billion. The case was still pending in October 2026. In March the tribunal decided to hear Honduras's objections to its power over the case together with the main dispute. Honduras filed its written defence on 12 July, the United States filed a written submission on 7 October, and on 22 October the tribunal issued an order about a site visit. The zone continues to operate during the dispute.
The case teaches what such a grant is worth. A country can give away lawmaking powers, and a later government and its courts can take them back. What the company holds is a right to seek money, under a treaty, if the taking breaks a promise. That is a large threat for a poor country, and critics and supporters disagree over whether it should exist. It does not amount to sovereignty for the zone.

set.laws: Own civil and commercial regulations, single-digit taxes, private arbitration with retired Arizona judges; Honduran criminal law still applies

sark.story:
Sark is a small island in the Channel Islands, off the coast of Normandy, with about 500 people on 5.44 square kilometres, counting the neighbouring islet of Brecqhou. Cars are banned from its roads, and people use tractors, bicycles and horse-drawn carts. It is part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a self-governing Crown Dependency, a territory that belongs to the British Crown but is not part of the United Kingdom. It had a form of government that stayed feudal into the 21st century, and that is why it is here.
In 1565 Queen Elizabeth I granted it to Helier de Carteret, of Jersey, as a fief, land held from the Crown in return for service. His conditions were to clear out pirates and keep at least 40 loyal men there, so he rented out 40 plots called tenements. The arrangement stuck. The island's parliament, Chief Pleas, long consisted of the Seigneur, or feudal lord, the Seneschal, a judge, the 40 tenement holders and 12 elected deputies. So most seats went with land ownership. Its laws are based on Norman law.
The challenge came from outsiders who bought in. The billionaire brothers David and Frederick Barclay bought Brecqhou in 1993. In the mid-1990s they went to the European Court of Human Rights to challenge Sark's inheritance law, which required their island to pass to David's eldest son. Women gained equal inheritance rights in 1999. The brothers then argued that the whole system broke the European Convention on Human Rights, the treaty that protects basic rights in Europe. The Privy Council, the body that approves laws for Crown territories, approved reforms on 9 April 2008, and the first elections under them were held that December. The new Chief Pleas has elected members, the Seneschal and the Seigneur, who may speak but not vote. There were 28 elected seats at first, cut to 18 in 2017 for lack of candidates. In form the Seigneur still holds the island as a fief from the Crown and remains lord of the manor, while the political powers that once went with that title have been abolished. Candidates backed by the brothers' businesses won few seats in the elections of 2008 and 2010.
Sark is a useful counterexample for anyone drawn to old charters and private islands. Its self-rule was real and lasted over four centuries, yet the rules of the larger legal system still reached it. Owning a small island gave the Barclays private land and a court case, and it gave them no power to run the place.

order-of-malta.story:
The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is the oldest and best-known answer to a question that runs through this whole subject, which is whether something can be sovereign without land. Sovereign means treated as an independent authority in international law, able to deal with states as an equal. The Order is a Catholic religious order with 39 vowed members, about 13,500 knights, dames and chaplains in all, and no territory of its own, and many countries treat it that way.
It began in the 11th century as a hospital community in Jerusalem, founded by a man known as Blessed Gerard, and Pope Paschal II approved it in 1113. As the Crusades went on it became a military order as well. It later ruled the island of Rhodes and then Malta, which it defended for more than three months against the Ottoman Empire in the Great Siege of 1565. For those centuries it was an ordinary territorial state.
In June 1798 Napoleon's forces took Malta and the Order lost its last territory. Then something unusual happened. Other countries went on treating it as a sovereign body, and it kept conducting diplomacy from its new base. It holds two headquarters buildings in Rome with extraterritorial status, meaning that Italian law treats them as outside normal Italian control, though they are not a territory the Order rules as a country. It also has a treaty with Malta, signed on 5 December 1998 and ratified in 2001, that lets it use the upper part of Fort St. Angelo in Birgu with limited extraterritoriality for 99 years. The fort stays under Malta's sovereignty, Malta may end the treaty after 50 years, the Order may not grant asylum there and Maltese courts generally keep full jurisdiction. So the one place on Malta it uses again comes by permission of the state that holds the island.
Day to day it does what a state's foreign ministry does. It issues its own passports, coins and stamps, and it signs treaties. Its website reports diplomatic relations with 118 countries and the European Union, while Wikipedia gives 115 states. The United Nations General Assembly made it a permanent observer in 1994, citing its humanitarian work. Only three of its senior officers count as its citizens, so no population depends on it. The rest of its members are citizens of ordinary countries. It says its diplomatic network exists to give its medical programmes protected access in crisis regions, and its hospitals and aid work supply the reason for states to keep the relationship going.
People who want a state without land often point to the Order. Its case is hard to copy. Its status rests on some nine centuries of history, on having once really ruled territory, on the Catholic Church's support and on a stream of aid work that governments value. Its recognition was inherited from a time when it held land, and no group has been shown to gain the same treatment from scratch. It shows that diplomatic recognition can outlast territory, as long as enough states choose to continue it.

somaliland.story:
Somaliland is a self-declared state in the Horn of Africa, on the Gulf of Aden, which has governed itself since 1991 while Somalia still claims it as its own. It covers 176,120 square kilometres and has about 6.2 million people. Its capital is Hargeisa. It is the leading example of a place that seems to meet the practical tests of statehood and still lacks wide recognition.
It was a British protectorate that united with Somalia in 1960, but the constitution put to a referendum in 1961 had little support in the north. Harsh policies against the Isaaq clan under Somalia's president Siad Barre led to a 10-year war. It ended with a declaration of independence in 1991, agreed at a large conference in Burao, as Somalia fell into civil war.
An interim government ran it at first. In 2002 it moved to a multi-party system, and in 2003 Dahir Riyale Kahin became its first elected president. It runs its own government and issues its own currency, the Somaliland shilling. Its parliament includes an upper House of Elders. It issues passports, and South Africa is reported to accept them. The New York Times reported that it has governed most of the land it claims largely in peace and stability. It belongs to the Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization, an advocacy group for those without a seat at the UN.
Statehood has usual tests, which are people, a defined territory, a government and the ability to deal with other states. Somaliland can point to all of them. Recognition, meaning other states accepting a place as a state, is a separate decision that each government takes for its own reasons. For decades none did so. Somaliland kept informal ties and hosted offices from Ethiopia and Taiwan. Taiwan and Somaliland signed a cooperation agreement in 2020 and exchanged offices, and whether they recognise each other is unclear.
On 26 December 2025 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu signed an agreement recognising it as an independent and sovereign state, making Israel the first UN member to do so. Several governments objected, among them Algeria and Azerbaijan, which said the step violated Somalia's sovereignty and unity. As of October 2026 Israel remained the only one. According to The New York Times, other governments fear recognition could encourage secession elsewhere.
The case shows the limits of building a state from within. Decades of order and elections have brought Somaliland contacts and one recognition. Wider recognition depends on the decisions of other governments.

set.laws: Interim government from 1991; multi-party system since 2002, with the first elected president in 2003

northern-cyprus.story:
Northern Cyprus is a self-declared state covering the northern third of the Mediterranean island of Cyprus, recognised as a country only by Turkey. It holds elections, has a president and a 50-member assembly, and has run itself for decades. It is the clearest example of a place with a government that the rest of the world has been told not to recognise.
Cyprus became independent from Britain in 1960 under a constitution that shared power between its Greek and Turkish communities, but violence between them soon followed. Many Greek Cypriots wanted enosis, union with Greece, and many Turkish Cypriots wanted the island partitioned. In 1974 a coup backed by Greece's military government, seeking to annex the island, prompted Turkey to invade and capture the north. Much of the Greek Cypriot population in the north was evicted, and Turkish Cypriots fled from the south. A 1975 agreement in Vienna arranged a population exchange.
In 1983 the north declared independence without agreement from the Republic of Cyprus, as the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. Resolution 541 of the UN Security Council, the UN's top body on peace and war, rejected the declaration as legally invalid and urged UN members not to recognise it. Other countries were asked to withhold acceptance even though the north held territory and ran a government. Other countries treat the area as Republic of Cyprus territory under Turkish military occupation.
Non-recognition has practical effects on everyday life. The Republic of Cyprus, as the recognised authority, has declared the north's airports and ports closed, so an international embargo applies, and trade goes through Turkey. The north uses the Turkish lira, which ties its economy to Turkey's. Because of this isolation it relies on Turkey for economic, political and military support. Some experts call it a puppet state, while others dispute that because of its separate elections and government.
A UN plan to reunite the island, known as the Annan Plan, went to a referendum in April 2004. About 65 percent of Turkish Cypriots voted for it and 76 percent of Greek Cypriots voted against it, so it failed and the division continues. The European Union, having admitted Cyprus as a member, pledged to end the north's isolation, and those pledges lost momentum. A UN buffer zone still divides the island, and Tufan Erhürman is the north's current president.
The case shows the weight of a Security Council call. Territory, people and a working government did not bring recognition, and one powerful supporter was enough to keep the place going without it.

white-rajahs-sarawak.story:
Sarawak is a territory on the north-west coast of Borneo, today a state of Malaysia. For 105 years it was ruled by a British family, the Brookes, who held the title of Rajah, a word for a king or prince. It is one of the few cases on record of a private person from abroad gaining a territory and ruling it as a monarch.
Before 1841 Sarawak was part of the realm of the Sultanate of Brunei, and owed loyalty to the sultan. James Brooke, a man of British origin born in India in 1803, helped the sultan's side fight piracy and uprisings among the local peoples. The sultan's representative, Pengiran Muda Hashim, promised him Sarawak in return for that help and then delayed. On 24 September 1841, after Brooke called on him with an armed ship, Hashim granted him the area around the town of Sarawak, now Kuching, and the nearby Bau mining district. Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II confirmed the appointment by July 1842. No price was paid, and in 1846 the sultan recognised Brooke's authority without requiring tribute.
Brooke rebuilt the government on the British model. He and his successor leased or annexed more land from Brunei until the state covered much of northern Borneo. James's will set the succession along the male line. His nephew Charles ruled from 1868 to 1917, and Charles's son Vyner from 1917 to 1946. In 1941, just before the Japanese invasion in the Second World War, Vyner ended the Rajah's absolute rule by giving new powers to the Council Negri, the local parliament.
After the Japanese occupation, Vyner ceded Sarawak to Britain as a Crown colony on 1 July 1946, citing a lack of money for reconstruction. Cession means a formal handing-over of territory. It was contested from the start. His nephew and legal heir, Anthony Brooke, objected, and so did most native members of the Council Negri. Because it was unclear whether the cession was legal, Britain also passed an annexation bill. An anti-cession movement grew, and the British governor Duncan Stewart was assassinated by members of a group seeking union with Indonesia. Sarawak became a British Crown colony, and in 1963 it became a state of Malaysia under the Malaysia Agreement.
The family's grant shows what such a position rested on. Brooke's title came from a ruler who had the power to give it and who owed him a favour, in a place where no stronger outside power objected. Other states took different positions on what Sarawak was. The United States had recognised it by 1850, and Britain appointed a consul and recognised it in 1864. The Netherlands refused. By a treaty of 14 June 1888 Sarawak became a state protected by Britain, governing itself at home while Britain ran its foreign relations and held a veto over any cession of its territory to a foreign state. The rule lasted as long as outside powers accepted it, and it ended when one family member signed it away over the objection of his heir and of the local parliament.

set.recognition: Recognised by the United States by 1850 and Britain in 1864; the Netherlands refused; a state protected by Britain from 1888

state-to-state-purchases.story:
A government holds more than ownership of land. It holds sovereignty, the legal right to make and enforce law over a territory. For centuries rulers treated that right as something that could be sold, and this entry gathers the recorded sales. A sale of this kind is done by treaty. Once it is complete, the buyer's laws apply, and people's ordinary land titles may carry on underneath.
The list is long and goes back to the Middle Ages. Scotland paid Norway 4,000 marks sterling, plus a yearly 100 marks, for the Isle of Man and the Hebrides in 1266. The United States paid France $15 million for Louisiana in 1803, about $7 per square kilometre, and Russia $7.2 million for Alaska in 1867, about $4 per square kilometre. Brazil paid Bolivia £2 million for Acre in 1903. The United States paid Denmark $25 million for the 400 square kilometres of the Danish West Indies, now the US Virgin Islands, in 1916, or $62,500 per square kilometre, and in the same deal recognised Danish sovereignty over all of Greenland. In 1958 Pakistan bought the port of Gwadar from Muscat and Oman. Accounts of that price differ, with the list giving 5.5 billion Pakistani rupees and other accounts about £3 million. The last sale on the list came in 1963, when West Germany paid the Netherlands 280 million Deutsche Marks for Elten, Selfkant and Suderwick, 69 square kilometres in all. The prices are those of the time and are not adjusted for inflation. The list covers purchases of territory, so leases do not appear on it.
Every buyer and every seller on the list is a state or a ruler, and no private person or company appears. That matters to anyone who dreams of buying a piece of the world and running it. A private buyer can buy land and hold a deed, as anyone can, but the deed gives ownership under the seller's law. The seller's police, courts and tax office still apply. To get sovereignty a buyer would need other governments to accept that it now rules there, and the list shows no case of that happening for a private buyer.
Greenland shows how the idea survives and where it stops. In 2019 Donald Trump, then in his first term as US president, said he wanted the United States to buy Greenland, and the Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, called the idea absurd. He cancelled a planned state visit to Denmark on 20 August 2019. In his second term he returned to it, and Danish and Greenlandic leaders answered that Greenland is not for sale and that its people have the right to decide their own future. The Greenlandic government stated that it chooses the Danish Realm over the United States. On 21 January 2026, speaking at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Trump said he would not use force and would not impose the tariffs he had set for 1 February as pressure over Greenland. He said a framework for a future deal on Greenland and the Arctic had been formed, and he named Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the envoy Steve Witkoff to handle the talks. The right of a people to decide their own status has become part of how such a transfer is judged, which earlier sales ignored. No sale between states appears on that list after 1963.

cocos-clunies-ross.story:
The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are a small group of coral atolls in the Indian Ocean, now an Australian territory, that one Scottish family ran for about 150 years. The islands were empty until the 1820s. John Clunies-Ross, a Scottish merchant seaman, stopped there in 1825 and put up a British flag. When he returned in 1827 with his family, he found an Englishman, Alexander Hare, already settled there with a party of people of Malay origin, including about 40 women. A feud followed. Hare's people drifted away from him, and he left and died in 1834.
Clunies-Ross began harvesting coconuts. Labour came from the Malay Peninsula, the Indonesian islands, Southern Africa and New Guinea, as indentured workers, slaves or convicts, and much of today's population descends from them. They were paid in the Cocos rupee, a currency the family minted itself that could be redeemed only at the company store. The family owned the land, the store and the money.
Britain annexed the islands in 1857 and made the family head its Superintendent. In 1886 Queen Victoria granted all the land to the family in perpetuity. Sovereignty, the right to rule the islands, stayed with Britain, which ran them as part of its Singapore colony. In practice the head of the family served as resident magistrate, so the landlord and the local government were the same man. In 1955 the islands became a territory of Australia, and the family remained the landowner.
Australia's attitude changed in the 1970s. In 1978, under threat of compulsory purchase, the family sold its property for A$6.25 million, apart from their home, Oceania House, and its grounds on Home Island. In 1983 the government told John Cecil Clunies-Ross to leave. The High Court of Australia ruled in 1984 that taking Oceania House had been unlawful. The government then stopped using his shipping company, which contributed to his bankruptcy. On 6 April 1984 all 261 eligible islanders voted in a United Nations-supervised Act of Self Determination, with 229 for full integration with Australia, 21 for free association, nine for independence and two giving no preference. Australia bought the last of his property in 1993 and sold Oceania House privately in 2001. A parliamentary report put the population at around 600, most of them Cocos Malays on Home Island.
The family's long hold ended within a few years of Australia deciding to buy it out.

tuvalu-digital-nation.story:
Tuvalu is a recognised Pacific country of about 10,000 people, spread over low-lying islands that the United Nations Development Programme classes as extremely vulnerable to climate change. The Rising Nations Initiative says that small island nations such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Marshall Islands are likely to become uninhabitable within a few decades. That raises a question international law has never had to answer, which is what happens to a country when its land goes under water.
The usual test for a state, set out in the 1933 Montevideo Convention, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the ability to deal with other states. Territory is on that list. So on one reading Tuvalu could lose its legal existence along with its homes. At the COP27 climate conference in November 2022 its Foreign Minister, Simon Kofe, appeared in a video standing knee deep in the ocean.
He said the country would move its land, ocean and culture to the cloud, as what it called the first digital nation. The plan, part of the Future Now Project, is to map all 124 islands and islets and to record cultural objects, language, elders' stories and dances, so that people abroad and future generations can keep them. The legal step is the more important one.
Tuvalu has asked other countries to agree in advance that it stays a state whatever happens to its land. Australia's Law Society Journal reported that 26 countries, including New Zealand and Australia, had legally recognised its digital statehood by December 2023, with a goal of 50. Australia also offered residency to 280 Tuvaluans a year. In its climate advisory opinion of July 2025 the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' top court, said that the disappearance of one of a state's parts "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood".
An advisory opinion does not bind states, though it carries weight. The land is still there and the question has not been tested. The case differs from every self-declared internet nation in one way. Tuvalu starts as a full state with UN membership and is seeking to keep that status, so the digital record is a supplement to recognition it already has. States may be able to keep an existing state in being by agreement. Nothing in this case lets a new state be created online.

set.pop: About 10,000 people in the physical country, though one source says about 12,000; the digital version has no residents

seasteading-institute.story:
A seastead is a permanent home at sea. The Seasteading Institute is an American non-profit that promotes them, founded on 15 April 2008 by Wayne Gramlich and Patri Friedman because they wanted room to try new forms of government. The basic argument comes from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. A country's exclusive economic zone, where it controls resources, runs 200 nautical miles from shore. Beyond it lie the high seas, which fall under no country's law apart from that of a ship's flag state, the country it is registered in. The founders proposed using that space.
Peter Thiel, a co-founder of PayPal, gave $500,000. The founders hoped to float a prototype in San Francisco Bay by 2010 and a seastead by 2014, and they met neither target. In January 2009 the institute patented ClubStead, a design for a 200-person resort about the size of a city block. In July 2009 Friedman launched Ephemerisle, a floating gathering in the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta inside California, which continued without him.
The institute later turned to working inside a country's waters, with a government's agreement. On 13 January 2017 it signed a memorandum of understanding, a non-binding agreement, with French Polynesia for a floating island prototype with partial self-rule. This changed the idea a good deal, since a host would now be granting the freedom. As local opposition grew, the government said in early 2018 that the agreement was not a legal document and had expired at the end of 2017. Blue Frontiers, a company the institute had set up for the project, then looked for another host, and its attempt in November 2018 to raise $3 million through a cryptocurrency failed.
No one lives on an institute seastead. It was still publishing in 2024, promoting safety standards after the death of Samuele Landi, who had planned a floating platform in the Indian Ocean. The institute's history shows the gap between the legal theory, which looks wide open, and the practical needs of waves, money and neighbouring governments. Its one real deal needed permission, and permission was withdrawn.

add_sources.t: French Polynesia sinks floating island project, RNZ, 28 Feb 2018

bantustans-transkei-bophuthatswana.story:
Bantustans, also called homelands, were territories that South Africa's white-minority government set aside for black people under apartheid, its system of legal racial separation. There were ten in South Africa, and four of them were declared independent countries. Most attempts to found a territory start with outsiders pushing against a state. Here a powerful state created the new countries itself, and anti-apartheid movements and every other government rejected them.
The background goes back to 1913, when governments began setting aside reserves for the black population. After the National Party came to power in 1948, Hendrik Verwoerd, first as minister for native affairs and then as prime minister, turned this into a plan. He argued that the reserves were the original homes of South Africa's black peoples. They came to about 13% of the country's land, and the rest was kept for the white minority. The Bantu Self-Government Act of 1959 set out a path for each homeland to become self-governing and then nominally independent. Supporters coined the word Bantustan as a comparison with the partition of India and Pakistan, and it soon became an insult.
The purpose was citizenship. The Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act of 1970 declared black South Africans to be citizens of these homelands, whether or not they had ever lived there, which took away their South African citizenship and the few rights it still gave them. If every black person belonged to a foreign state, South Africa would have no duty to give them a vote. In 1978 the minister Connie Mulder told parliament that, if the policy was carried through, there would be not one black man with South African citizenship. An estimated 3.5 million people were forced from their homes from the 1960s to the 1980s, many of them moved into the Bantustans.
South Africa declared four homelands independent, Transkei in 1976, Bophuthatswana in 1977, Venda in 1979 and Ciskei in 1981. Transkei served as the testing ground for the policy. Each had a government and a constitution set up under South African law. Laws differed from those in South Africa, and wealthy South Africans made use of that, for example by building large casinos such as Sun City in Bophuthatswana, where gambling could be offered.
Recognition is when other states accept a place as a state, and it is what these places could not get. On 26 October 1976 the UN General Assembly, in resolution 31/6 A, called on all governments to deny Transkei any form of recognition and to have no dealings with it or other bantustans. That December the Security Council, in Resolution 402, recalled this when South Africa closed border posts to pressure Lesotho into recognising Transkei, and it noted with appreciation that Lesotho had refused. Anti-apartheid movements and every foreign government refused. Only South Africa treated them as countries, along with the four themselves, which recognised one another. They had the outward parts of a state, including territory, people and officials, and that was not enough, because other governments saw them as a device for carrying out apartheid.
In 1985 President P. W. Botha said black people in South Africa proper would no longer lose their citizenship in this way, and that citizens of the independent homelands could reapply for it. The Interim Constitution that came with the end of apartheid in 1994 effectively abolished the Bantustans, and they were absorbed back into South Africa. The ending met resistance. General Constand Viljoen sent about 1,500 militiamen to protect Bophuthatswana's leader, Lucas Mangope, and contest the end of its status, and white far-right groups such as the Afrikaner Weerstandsbeweging backed the homeland leaders. Bophuthatswana was reincorporated into South Africa on 27 April 1994. For anyone founding a territory, the case shows that a declaration of independence, even with the full support of the neighbouring power, does not make a state in the eyes of others.

bougainville-2019.story:
Bougainville is an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the South Pacific, made up mainly of a large island east of the main country and north of the Solomon Islands. It voted for independence in 2019 and is still waiting for it. The case shows how a peace deal can promise a vote without promising what follows.
Talk of leaving is old. In 1968 Bougainville's members in the territorial assembly proposed a vote on staying with Papua New Guinea, joining the Solomon Islands or going independent, and no vote was held. Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia in 1975, and Bougainville was made a province in 1976. In 1988 tension turned into civil war between the Bougainville Revolutionary Army and government forces, and one key issue was the Panguna copper mine, which closed in 1989. The war ended with a ceasefire in 1998 and the 2001 Bougainville Peace Agreement. That agreement created the Autonomous Bougainville Government and required a referendum some 10 to 15 years after that government's first election.
The vote ran from 23 November to 7 December 2019 and offered a choice of greater autonomy or independence. Independence won 176,928 votes to 3,043, or 98.31 percent, with turnout of 87.38 percent, though press and parliamentary reports in 2026 give the share as 97.7 percent. It was not binding. Under the peace agreement Papua New Guinea's national parliament has the final decision, so the people wanting to leave depend on the votes of those they are leaving.
The wait has been long. In July 2021 the two governments agreed that Bougainville would become independent by 2027, subject to that parliament's approval. In July 2026 a forum of Bougainville leaders recommended 1 September 2030 as the target date. The result was finally tabled in parliament on 27 August 2026. Opposition leader James Nomane complained that MPs had only just received the documents. Prime Minister James Marape said the two governments would meet in October to set a date for the vote. Some MPs fear other provinces might follow, a fear the committee chair Allan Marat called uninformed.
Even a yes would not end the matter. Minister Manasseh Makiba said a yes vote would start a transitional phase of self-government under a plan called the Melanesian Framework and would not bring immediate independence. The two governments could not agree on what happens if parliament votes no. The majority required is also disputed. The national government says two-thirds or three-quarters of an absolute majority, the governing coalition has asked for 89 of the 118 MPs, and the Bougainville government argues for 60 seats. AAP, an Australian news agency, reports that Bougainville's government plans to declare sovereignty by 2030 if parliament delays further. Parliament opened its debate on the result in the week of 20 October 2026, with Makiba speaking first. Marape said a date would be decided together with the Bougainville leadership. As of 22 October no vote had been held and no date had been set.

add_sources.t: PNG MPs given two days to debate Bougainville referendum results, PINA, 15 Oct 2026
PNG parliament urged to balance Bougainville independence with national unity, PINA, 22 Oct 2026

denard-comoros.story:
Bob Denard was a French mercenary, a soldier for hire, who took part in four attempts to change the government of the Comoros between 1975 and 1995. The Comoros is a small group of islands in the Indian Ocean, between Mozambique and Madagascar, and a former French colony. It has seen more than twenty coups in recent decades. For long periods Denard was its real military power, which makes him one of the few private soldiers who came close to owning a country.
Denard had fought in the Congo and elsewhere in Africa, and for most of his career he had the unofficial backing of France and its secret service, which wanted to keep its influence in its former colonies. On 6 July 1975 President Ahmed Abdallah declared the islands independent on his own initiative. Denard then removed him, on the orders of Jacques Foccart, who had coordinated President de Gaulle's African policy, and Ali Soilih replaced him.
Soilih turned towards socialist politics. On 13 May 1978 Denard returned with 43 men, backed by the government of Rhodesia, and overthrew him, and Soilih was killed on 29 May. The official account that he was shot while trying to escape is not generally believed. Abdallah came back as president.
For the next 11 years Denard held the arrangement together from inside. He commanded the 500-strong presidential guard, became a citizen and acquired hotels and land. The islands also suited outside interests. Denard used them as a base for operations in Mozambique and Angola, and France used them as a way around the embargo on apartheid South Africa. He held the force, while the recognised government remained Abdallah's, so other countries dealt with the president.
In 1989, fearing a coup, Abdallah signed an order for Denard's guard to disarm the regular army. Shortly afterwards he was shot in his office, allegedly by a military officer, and Denard was injured in the same incident. French prosecutors later alleged that Abdallah was killed on Denard's orders because he was about to dismiss him. Denard and another man, Dominique Malacrino, were acquitted of the murder for lack of evidence, after Abdallah's family dropped its suit. A few days after the shooting Denard agreed to leave after talks with French representatives, and French paratroopers took him to South Africa.
On 27 September 1995 he landed again with 30 to 33 men against President Djohar. This time France was against him. The French army intervened and ended the attempt on 4 October, and he surrendered. A French court gave him a five-year suspended sentence in June 2006. On appeal in July 2007 this became four years with three suspended, which he never served because of poor health. Witnesses at the trial said French intelligence had supported him. He died in October 2007.
The case shows the limit of a very small armed force. Forty-three men could take a weak state. Keeping it depended on a large outside power allowing it, and when France opposed him in 1995 the landing lasted about a week.

sahrawi-republic.story:
The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic is a government in exile for Western Sahara, a desert territory on the Atlantic coast of north-west Africa, most of which Morocco holds. It has more diplomatic standing than almost any other unrecognised state, and it has little control of the land it claims.
The territory was a Spanish colony from 1884, known as Spanish Sahara. In December 1974 the UN General Assembly asked the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, whether the land had belonged to no one when Spain colonised it and, if not, what legal ties it had with Morocco and with what the court called the Mauritanian entity.
The court answered on 16 October 1975. It said the land had not belonged to no one. It found ties of allegiance between the Sultan of Morocco and some of the tribes, and rights, some of them over land, linking the territory with the Mauritanian entity. It found no tie of territorial sovereignty, meaning no right to rule the land, with either one, and it said the ties it did find did not change the rule that the territory's people should decide their own future.
Later in 1975 Spain left and handed administration to Morocco and Mauritania under the Madrid Accords. The Polisario Front, a movement seeking an independent state for the Sahrawi people, proclaimed the republic on 27 February 1976 at Bir Lehlou.
War followed. Mauritania withdrew in 1979, and Morocco built a 2,700-kilometre sand wall dividing the territory. The republic claims 266,000 square kilometres and controls about 90,000 east of the wall, a share given as anywhere from a fifth to 30 percent. It calls that the Liberated Territories, and Morocco calls the rest its Southern Provinces. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991 promised a referendum, which never took place because the two sides dispute who may vote. Polisario declared the ceasefire over in November 2020.
Daily life is largely in exile. The official capital, Laayoune, is held by Morocco, and the temporary capital is Tifariti. Most day-to-day government runs from the Rabuni refugee camp near Tindouf, in Algeria, where about 173,600 people lived in 2023, with about 40,000 in the held areas as of 2010. So a government works from another country's soil. The Sahrawi peseta exists on paper, and people use Moroccan dirhams, Algerian dinars, Mauritanian ouguiyas and euros.
It is a full member of the African Union, and counts of recognition range from 33 to 46 UN members, and many others have withdrawn or suspended it. The United States recognised Moroccan sovereignty in December 2020. On 31 October 2025 the Security Council voted 11 in favour for talks based on Morocco's autonomy plan. Polisario said the resolution does not imply recognition of Moroccan rule and that it will not join talks aimed at legitimising it. In 2026 Mali said it was withdrawing recognition. The UN still lists Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory, one whose people have not yet governed themselves.
Some other breakaway places, such as Abkhazia in the Caucasus, control their land and have very few recognitions. The Sahrawi government has the reverse position, with recognitions and a seat in a regional body and little of the land. Recognition can also shrink, as governments withdraw it one at a time.

add_sources.t: Western Sahara, advisory opinion of 16 October 1975, International Court of Justice

chagos-treaty-2025.story:
The Chagos Archipelago is a group of islands in the Indian Ocean. Britain ran it as part of its colony of Mauritius until 1965. That year, before Mauritius became independent, Britain separated the islands to create the British Indian Ocean Territory. On 23 September 1965 the British Prime Minister, Harold Wilson, told the Mauritian premier, Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, that he could go home with independence or without it. The Mauritian side accepted the separation for up to £3 million and promises that the islands would return when no longer needed. That December the UN General Assembly asked Britain to do nothing that would divide Mauritius, by a vote of 89 to none, with Britain among those abstaining.
About 1,360 people lived on the islands when the territory was created. Between 1967 and 1973 Britain stopped islanders who had left from going back and removed the rest to Mauritius and Seychelles. The last ship left Peros Banhos atoll on 26 May 1973. Diego Garcia, one of the islands, became the site of a joint British and American military base.
An advisory opinion is a court's answer to a legal question from a UN body, and it is not a judgment against a party. In February 2019 the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, advised, 13 to 1, that decolonisation had not been lawfully completed and that Britain should end its administration as rapidly as possible. The court held that Mauritius could not validly consent to the detachment while under British authority, and that the separation had not rested on the free and genuine will of the people. The General Assembly then demanded, by 116 votes to 6, that Britain withdraw within six months. Britain treated the opinion as not legally binding and stayed.
On 22 May 2025 the two prime ministers signed an agreement. Mauritius would hold sovereignty, the right to rule, over the whole archipelago and would authorise Britain to use its rights over Diego Garcia for an initial 99 years. Britain would pay £165 million a year for the first three years and £120 million a year after that. The United States, India and the African Union welcomed it, while the Conservatives, Reform UK and some Chagossians objected.
On 16 February 2026 four Chagossians, accompanied by a former Conservative member of parliament, landed without permits on Île du Coin in the Peros Banhos atoll, intending to settle. The territory's Chief Justice, James Lewis, blocked their removal. On 31 March 2026 he quashed the 2004 rule that no person has a right to live in the territory. He also held that the group was on the island illegally and had gained no right to a permanent camp. His decision was put on hold during an appeal, which the territory's Court of Appeal heard in London on 15 to 17 July 2026. Six Chagossians were still living on the island in September. No ruling on the appeal is known.
Ratification, the final step that makes a signed treaty binding, stalled in 2026. On 14 April a British minister told the House of Commons that a change in the American president's position made it impossible to agree an update to the 1966 British and American agreement, and that the implementing bill would not pass. It lapsed that month. In September the new British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he would work towards a resolution, and the Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said the deal could not proceed without American support and that the payments would not go ahead at this stage. As of October 2026 the treaty had been signed and had not entered into force.
chagos-treaty-2025.mechanism: A treaty can move sovereignty from one state to another while the old ruler keeps the use of one island for a set period. Until it is ratified, the existing arrangement stays in place.

add_sources.t: Chagos Islands deal on hold after lack of US support, ITV News, 23 Sep 2026
Resettlement of Île du Coin, Wikipedia
Mandarin v Commissioner of BIOT, judgment of 31 March 2026, BIOT Supreme Court
L'autodétermination au coeur des débats devant la Cour d'appel, allAfrica, 17 Jul 2026

nottebohm-icj.story:
Nationality is the legal bond between a person and a country. It matters here because of who may speak up for a person abroad. A country can bring a claim against another country on someone's behalf only through that bond.
Friedrich Nottebohm was a German national who settled in Guatemala in 1905 and lived and did business there for decades. In October 1939, just after the Second World War began, he obtained the nationality of Liechtenstein while on a visit to Europe, and he returned to Guatemala in 1940. Liechtenstein was neutral in the war, and the court found that the only purpose of the grant was to give him the standing of a neutral citizen. In 1943 Guatemala removed him under war measures.
Liechtenstein took Guatemala to the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, and claimed compensation for him. The Court overruled Guatemala's first objection in November 1953, and on 6 April 1955 it held Liechtenstein's claim inadmissible, meaning that it would not hear the claim at all.
The Court said that on the international plane a grant of nationality is entitled to recognition by other states only if it represents a genuine connection between the state and the person. Nottebohm had no such connection with Liechtenstein at the time of the grant. His ties were with Guatemala and Germany.
The ruling is narrow, and people often stretch it. It concerned whether Liechtenstein could protect him against Guatemala. It did not say he stopped being a Liechtenstein national in Liechtenstein's law. In a 2025 case, Commission v Malta, the EU's Court of Justice ruled against Malta for selling citizenship. The Maltese government argued that a duty of prior genuine link cannot be drawn from Nottebohm, and the court decided the case on the basis of EU law. For anyone buying a passport to escape a country, the new passport may be weakest against the country where the person actually lives.
